objectives: Use excludability and rivalry to classify private goods, public goods, and common resources.
Explain why the free-rider problem keeps markets from supplying enough public goods, and describe the role of government.
Explain why the tragedy of the commons happens, and compare solutions such as property rights, permits and quotas, and limits on use.

concepts.definition: A good is excludable if people who have not paid can be prevented from using it. If they cannot be kept out, the good is nonexcludable.
A good is rival if one person's use reduces the amount available to others. If use by one person does not reduce what others can use, the good is nonrival.
A good that is both nonexcludable and nonrival, such as national defense, streetlights, or basic research. Because it is hard to charge for, the market tends not to supply enough of it.

Because people can enjoy a benefit without paying for it, each person tries to avoid paying, and as a result a public good that would help everyone is not produced, or is produced in too small an amount.
A resource that is nonexcludable but rival, such as fish in the ocean, a shared pasture, or the atmosphere. Anyone can use it, but using it leaves less for others.
When each user of a common resource looks only at their own gain and ignores the harm done to others, the resource is overused and can be depleted.

beginner.summary: A public good, like a streetlight, is something you can't keep nonpayers from using and that doesn't run out when people share it. A common resource, like fish in the sea, is something anyone can take, but taking it leaves less for others.

sections.heading: Can you keep people out? Does sharing use it up?
paragraphs: You have to pay before you can take a loaf of bread (people can be kept out), and once you eat it, no one else can (it gets used up). Most things we buy in stores work this way: people can be kept out, and sharing uses them up. Economists call the first property excludability and the second rivalry. A good that has them is called excludable and rival.

sections.heading: Public goods everyone shares
paragraphs: What about a streetlight on your block? You can't light up only the houses that paid for it and leave the others in the dark. And when you walk under it, there is no less light for anyone else. A good like this is called a public good.

Because you can use a public good without paying, it is tempting to wait and think, "Someone else will pay for it." This is called free riding. If everyone thinks that way, a streetlight that would help everyone might never go up. That is why public goods such as streetlights, national defense, and fire protection are often paid for by the government through taxes.

sections.heading: Common resources: open to all, but they run out
paragraphs: Anyone can catch fish in the ocean, but when one person catches a lot, there are fewer fish left for others. Something like this is called a common resource. If every fisher thinks, "If I don't catch them, someone else will, so I'd better catch them first," the fish never get a chance to recover, and in the end everyone loses. This is called the tragedy of the commons.
Clean air and a stable climate work much like common resources. Everyone uses them, but the more greenhouse gases we release, the less of a stable climate there is for everyone.

intermediate.summary: Classifying goods by excludability and rivalry shows that public goods are undersupplied because of free riding, while common resources are overused because of the tragedy of the commons.

sections.heading: Sorting goods by two criteria
paragraphs: Goods can be sorted by excludability (can nonpayers be kept out?) and rivalry (does one person's use reduce what others can use?). Excludable and rival goods are private goods (bread, clothing); nonexcludable and nonrival goods are public goods (national defense, streetlights); nonexcludable but rival goods are common resources (ocean fish, a shared pasture). The same good can become more or less excludable depending on technology and institutions (for example, a toll road versus a free road).

sections.heading: Free riding and the undersupply of public goods
paragraphs: Because people who do not pay for a public good cannot be kept out, it is hard to recover its cost through sales. Each individual has an incentive to rely on others' contributions and simply enjoy the benefit, so voluntary contributions fall short of the good's true value. The social value of a public good is the sum of the values all users receive, and even when that sum exceeds the cost, the market may not supply it. That is why governments commonly collect taxes to provide public goods. Sometimes the market finds a way, as with broadcasting paid for by advertising.

sections.heading: The tragedy of the commons and its solutions
paragraphs: Users of a common resource look only at what they gain and ignore the losses others suffer as the resource shrinks. This is a negative externality imposed on other users. Solutions include assigning property rights so that an owner has a reason to conserve, handing out permits or quotas, and limiting how much can be taken or when. How well each works depends on monitoring costs, whether the allocation is fair, and whether people are willing to follow the rules.

advanced.summary: The social marginal benefit of a public good is the sum of every user's marginal benefit. With a common resource, entry continues as long as the average harvest exceeds cost, so the resource is used beyond the efficient level, which is set by the marginal harvest.

sections.heading: Nonrivalry and the vertical sum of demand
paragraphs: Each unit of a private good is used by only one person, so market demand adds up individual quantities demanded horizontally. Each unit of a public good is used by everyone at once, so its social value is the vertical sum of the values all users place on it. With n users, the social marginal benefit is MSB = MB₁ + MB₂ + … + MBₙ, and the efficient quantity is where MSB = MC. Each person looks only at their own MB and refuses to pay when MB < MC, so the good may go unsupplied even when the sum exceeds MC.

sections.heading: The logic of free riding
paragraphs: If each person reasons, "Whether or not I pay, I get to use it as long as someone else supplies it," then not paying is the better choice for each individual. If everyone reasons the same way, the public good is not supplied. Everyone would be better off cooperating, yet each person's rational choice leads to a worse outcome. This structure is the same as the prisoner's dilemma. Compulsory contributions, such as taxes, are one way out of the dilemma.

sections.heading: Overuse of common resources and the climate
paragraphs: In an open-access fishery, a boat enters whenever its average catch is worth more than its cost. For society as a whole, however, what matters is how much the total catch rises when that boat enters (the marginal catch). If F(n) is the total catch of n boats and w is the cost of one boat, free entry continues as long as the average F(n)/n ≥ w, while the efficiency condition is that the marginal catch F(n) − F(n − 1) ≥ w. The catch a new boat takes away from other boats does not enter that boat's cost, so entry goes beyond the efficient level (worked example 3).

The atmosphere is like a common resource that absorbs greenhouse gases, and cutting emissions to stabilize the climate is like a global public good that benefits every country. So climate action faces both free riding and the tragedy of the commons at once, which makes cooperation between countries difficult.

worked_examples.title: Splitting the cost of a streetlight
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: It costs $6,000 to put up a streetlight on a block with 30 households. If every household pays an equal share, how much does each household pay?
worked_examples.answer: $200 per household. But since households can use the light without paying, some are likely to try not to pay.

worked_examples.title: The value exceeds the cost, so why isn't it built?
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: Each of the 30 households on the block above values the streetlight at $300. What is its total value to society, and how does that compare with the $6,000 cost? Why might a voluntary fundraiser still fail?
steps: Everyone uses a public good at the same time, so its social value = 30 × $300 = $9,000.
$9,000 > $6,000, so building it is a gain for society (net benefit of $3,000).
But each household thinks, "If the others pay, I can use it without paying," and tries to avoid paying (free riding).
worked_examples.answer: The social value of $9,000 exceeds the $6,000 cost, but free riding may leave the fundraiser short. That is why such goods are often paid for jointly, for example through taxes.

worked_examples.title: How many boats will enter the fishery?
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: In a fishery, the total daily catch (in tons) by number of boats is 10 for 1 boat, 18 for 2, 24 for 3, 28 for 4, and 30 for 5. The daily cost of running one boat equals the value of 5 tons of fish. If anyone can enter, how many boats will enter? Which number of boats maximizes society's net catch?
steps: Average catch per boat: 10, 9, 8, 7, 6. All five exceed the cost of 5, so with free entry 5 boats enter.
Marginal catch (the increase from adding one more boat): 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. Only the first 3 boats add at least 5.
Net catch = total catch − 5 × number of boats: with 3 boats, 24 − 15 = 9; with 5 boats, 30 − 25 = 5.
Free entry reduces society's net catch by 9 − 5 = 4 tons.
worked_examples.answer: With free entry, 5 boats enter, but the efficient number is 3. Overuse lowers the net catch by 4 tons per day.

real_world_examples.title: Who supplies public goods?
paragraphs: Public goods such as national defense, basic research, and public health are hard to withhold from people who have not paid, so in many countries the government provides them using tax revenue. In some cases, though, the market finds a way to supply services with public-good features, as with broadcasting funded by advertising.

real_world_examples.title: Overfishing and catch quotas
paragraphs: Fisheries that anyone can enter are prone to overfishing. To prevent this, governments use fishing licenses, limits on the total catch, and systems that assign each boat a share of the allowed catch.

real_world_examples.title: Climate change: an externality that crosses borders
paragraphs: Global warming is an international externality that no single country can solve on its own. Countries with different income levels and priorities find it hard to agree on emission cuts, and even with international agreements such as the 2015 Paris Agreement, participation and follow-through remain ongoing challenges.

sdg_case.title: How should our city spend its climate budget?
paragraphs: SDG target 13.2 calls for integrating climate change measures into policies and planning, and SDG target 7.2 calls for substantially increasing the share of renewable energy.

Hypothetical situation: A city has set aside a climate budget. Cutting greenhouse gases has the features of a public good: everyone benefits, but no one wants to pay the cost alone. The city council has to rank three projects.

options.name: Expand bike-share and bus routes (provided directly by the city)
benefits: More public services that all residents can share.
Car use and emissions may fall.
costs: The effect is small in areas where few people ride.
assumptions: Residents actually use them instead of driving.

options.name: Install solar panels on schools and public buildings
benefits: The share of renewable energy rises (SDG 7.2), and electricity bills fall.
Students can use the panels for energy education.
costs: The upfront installation cost is high.
assumptions: The equipment lasts a long time, and the electricity it produces is not wasted.

options.name: A voluntary citizen energy-saving campaign
benefits: It raises awareness of and interest in climate issues (SDG 13.3).
costs: Free riding may keep participation low.
Its effect is hard to measure.
assumptions: Many residents change their behavior on their own.

discussion: Which of the three projects best avoids the free-rider problem, and which is the fairest? If the two criteria point to different projects, how would you decide?

key_takeaways: Classifying goods by excludability and rivalry gives private goods (excludable and rival), public goods (nonexcludable and nonrival), and common resources (nonexcludable but rival).
Because of free riding, markets tend to undersupply public goods, so they are often paid for jointly, for example through taxes.

When each user looks only at their own gain, a common resource is overused and depleted (the tragedy of the commons). Property rights, permits, quotas, and limits on use are possible solutions, and the climate is an example of this problem on a global scale.
